name: Antioch
info: Antioch was a city on the Orontes River in northern Syria, on the site of modern Antakya in Turkey. Founded in 300 BCE by Seleucus I, it was a Seleucid capital, the capital of Roman Syria and the centre of a Crusader principality.

facts.founded: Founded by Seleucus I Nicator in 300 BCE, after his victory at Ipsus in 301 BCE; John Malalas gives 22 May 300 BCE for his sacrifice to Zeus at the site.
facts.where: On the left bank of the Orontes, beneath Mount Silpius, in the southwest Amuq plain, in Hatay Province in southern Turkey.
facts.known: The Seleucid capital; the capital of Roman Syria; one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire; an early centre of Christianity and one of the five original patriarchates; the suburb of Daphne; the Antioch mosaics; the Crusader Principality of Antioch; repeated earthquakes
facts.today: The ancient city lies mostly buried beneath the modern city of Antakya in Hatay Province, Turkey.

t: Seleucus I founded Antioch in 300 BCE, and it was the capital of the Seleucid Empire and then of Roman Syria, where it may have had over 500,000 inhabitants at its peak.
It was a chief centre of early Christianity, the place where the name Christian is said in the New Testament to have first emerged, and the seat of one of the five original patriarchates.
Earthquakes, Persian sacks in 256 and 540, the Crusader and Mamluk wars and a change in trade routes reduced it, and after Baybars took it in 1268 it never recovered its size.
dyk: In 1432 there were only about 300 inhabited houses within the walls of a city that had held, at its peak, perhaps over 500,000 people.
ev: After the Battle of Ancyra, Antioch becomes the main centre of the Seleucid Empire
Antioch passes with Syria to the Roman Republic
A huge earthquake strikes while Trajan is in the city
Khosrow I destroys Antioch and deports its people to Persian Mesopotamia
Byzantine forces capture the city after a siege
The Crusaders take Antioch after a siege of eight months
Baybars captures and razes the city

sections.origins:
Antioch stood in the southwest Amuq plain, a fertile lowland watered by three rivers, between the slopes of Mount Silpius and the left bank of the Orontes, at an elevation of 90 metres. The plain connected Anatolia, Syria, the Mediterranean Sea and the deserts of the Middle East, and it had been inhabited for thousands of years before the city. Bronze Age sites there included Tell Atchana and Tell Tayinat. Cyrus the Great conquered the region in the mid-sixth century BCE, and it remained under the Achaemenid Empire until Alexander the Great invaded in 333 BCE.

The writers Libanius and John Malalas connected the site with Greek legends of earlier settlements, among them Iopolis, Kasiotis and Herakleia, and Libanius held that Alexander had meant to found a city there. There is no proof for any of these claims. After Seleucus defeated Antigonus I at Ipsus in 301 BCE he ordered the foundation of four settlements between 301 and 299 BCE: Seleucia Pieria and Laodicea on the coast, Antioch and Apamea inland. According to Malalas and Libanius an eagle carried sacrificial meat to the future site of Antioch, showing the place Zeus favoured. Scholars now hold that the city was named for Seleucus' father Antiochus, not for his son of the same name.
sections.growth:
The original city was laid out in imitation of the grid plan of Alexandria by the architect Xenarius. The citadel stood on Mount Silpius, and two great colonnaded streets crossed in the centre. Antiochus I Soter added a second walled area, Seleucus II Callinicus a third on an island in the Orontes, and Antiochus IV Epiphanes a fourth, after which Antioch was known as the Tetrapolis. According to ancient tradition 5,500 Athenians and Macedonians were settled there with an unknown number of native Syrians, and the free Greek settlers with their families probably numbered between 17,000 and 25,000. Its importance dates chiefly from the Battle of Ancyra in 240 BCE.

Under Rome the city grew larger still. Julius Caesar visited in 47 BCE, a Roman forum was laid out, and Tiberius built colonnades. Antoninus Pius paved the great east to west street with granite, and baths and aqueducts were built, the finest aqueduct by Hadrian. The hippodrome measured more than 490 metres in length and could hold up to 80,000 spectators. Antioch may have had over 500,000 inhabitants at its peak, making it the third largest city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria, and its walls, which first enclosed about 90 hectares, may have enclosed 500 hectares by 540 CE. Most of the surviving Antioch mosaics date from the fourth and fifth centuries, its golden age.
sections.rulers:
Seleucus I founded the city, and it was the capital of the western Seleucid Empire under Antiochus I and the Seleucid capital from 240 BCE until 63 BCE. The people took sides in the quarrels of the Seleucid house and rose in rebellion against Alexander Balas in 147 BCE and Demetrius II Nicator in 129 BCE. They invited Tigranes the Great to occupy the city in 83 BCE and petitioned Rome against the restoration of Antiochus XIII in 64 BCE. Antioch then passed with Syria to the Roman Republic, though it remained a civitas libera, and it became the capital of Roman Syria. From the early 4th century it was the seat of the comes Orientis, head of the Diocese of the East.

After the Persian sack of 540 and Persian conquest in 613 the city was taken in 637 by Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah of the Rashidun Caliphate. Byzantine forces recaptured it in 969 after a siege, and Suleiman ibn Qutalmish took it in 1084. The Crusaders conquered it in June 1098 and it became the centre of the Principality of Antioch, ruled by Bohemond, Tancred, Raymond of Poitiers and their successors, several times under regents and at times as a vassal of the Byzantine emperors. Baybars took it in 1268. It entered the Ottoman Empire in 1516 as a sub-province of Aleppo, and from 1831 to 1840 it was the headquarters of Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt.
sections.life:
Antioch's early population was a mix of local settlers, Macedonians and Jews, who were given full status from the beginning. In the Hellenistic period it was the main centre of Hellenistic Judaism at the end of the Second Temple period, and Jews lived in a quarter called the Kerateion. Outside the city lay the park of Daphne, about 8 kilometres south, with its springs and its temple of Apollo; its beauty and lax morals were celebrated across the ancient world. The city was known for its fertile plain, which produced wheat, barley, olives, oil and wine.

Antioch was a chief centre of early Christianity. The New Testament asserts that the name Christian first emerged there, and according to tradition Saint Peter was among the first missionaries. Ten assemblies of the church were held there between 252 and 300, and Constantine began the Great Church in 327. A school of Christian thought, led by Diodorus of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia, took its name from the city. In 362 Ammianus Marcellinus implied that pagans and Christians lived quite harmoniously, and the sophist Libanius and the preacher John Chrysostom lived there. In the Arab period Christians, Muslims and Jews lived together, with periods of tension, and Christians remained the dominant population until the Crusades.
sections.crises:
Antioch lay on the northern Dead Sea Rift and suffered more than sixty notable earthquakes, around ten of them above magnitude 7. John Malalas recorded one in 148 BCE that did immense damage. Others struck in 37, in 115, when Trajan took shelter in the circus and the population fell to less than 400,000, in 526 and 528, and in 588, when the Domus Aureus of Constantine was destroyed. The Orontes and the streams from Silpius also flooded the city regularly, and the alluvium came to bury it metres deep.

In 256 the Persians under Shapur I raided the city and many people were slain in the theatre. The city was burned, some 100,000 inhabitants were killed and the rest deported to Gundeshapur, and Valerian recaptured it the next year. In 540 Khosrow I completed the destruction begun by the earthquakes, deporting the people to a new city in Persian Mesopotamia, and Antioch lost as many as 300,000 people. Anti-Jewish riots broke out in 490 or 491, in which the Green faction attacked the Jews; the accounts differ on the details. Baybars took the city on 18 May 1268 and razed it, killing or enslaving nearly the entire population. In 1355 it still had a considerable population, but by 1432 only about 300 inhabited houses stood within its walls.
sections.legacy:
Antioch was called the cradle of Christianity because of its longevity and the role it played in the emergence of early Christianity. It became the seat of one of the five original patriarchates, and five churches still use the title of patriarch of Antioch for their prime bishops: the Syriac Orthodox Church, the Maronite, Syriac Catholic and Melkite Greek Catholic Churches, and the Greek Orthodox Church of Antioch. Most have moved their seats to Damascus, and the Maronite Church to Bkerké in Lebanon, which continues the Antiochene liturgical tradition. The Tyche of Antioch, a seated figure crowned with the city's walls and holding wheat stalks, with the Orontes swimming under her feet, became its civic symbol.

Little of the Roman city can be seen. The remains lie mostly beneath alluvial deposits from the Orontes, and what shows are the fortification walls on the mountains east of the modern city, several aqueducts and the Church of St Peter, said to have been a meeting place of an early Christian community. Excavations between 1932 and 1939 did not find Constantine's church or the imperial palace, but recovered nearly 300 mosaics from villas and baths in Antioch, Daphne and Seleucia Pieria. Many are in the Hatay Archaeology Museum in Antakya, and others hang in Princeton University Art Museum and the museums of the other sponsoring institutions.

summary: Antioch was founded in 300 BCE by Seleucus I on the Orontes, in what is now Antakya in southern Turkey. It was a Seleucid and Roman capital and an early centre of Christianity, and earthquakes, Persian sacks and the Crusader and Mamluk wars reduced it. Baybars razed it in 1268.
references: Klaus-Peter Todt, Dukat und griechisch-orthodoxes Patriarchat von Antiocheia in mittelbyzantinischer Zeit (969-1084) (Harrassowitz, 2020)
notes: No separate history article exists in the work folder; the city's own article was the only source.
START: the article says 'founded in 300 BC' and gives 23 April 300 for Seleucia Pieria and 22 May 300 for Antioch (the latter only as Malalas's account). I used -300 without circa.

CAPITAL: the article says Antioch became capital 'under Antiochus I' (so before 240 BCE), yet the lead says the Seleucid capital 'from 240 BC until 63 BC' and that its paramount importance dates from 240. Both are given; Seleucia was first designated capital of the Tetrapolis.

POPULATION: 'over 500,000 at its peak' (lead), 'more than half a million' under Augustus, Strabo implying about 300,000 free inhabitants, 'less than 400,000' after 115, Chrysostom's 200,000 dêmos, Libanius's 150,000 in 363. I used only the 500,000 peak (hedged 'may have') and the 115 figure. The figures are not mutually consistent; editor to read.

PERSIAN SACK: the article gives 256 (Shapur I, 100,000 killed) and 540 (Khosrow I, up to 300,000 lost), but also says Constantine's church 'stood until the Persian sack in 538'. I used 540 and left 538 out. In the crises section The article names no source for the 100,000 figure and the deportation to Gundeshapur, so they are stated plainly.

EARTHQUAKES: the article says the 1114 earthquake 'destroyed its foundations' (Roger of Salerno rebuilt); I left it out of the list. The article says 526 damaged Antioch and 528 'affected' it; 'destroyed' is used only for 588.
1268: 'killing or enslaving nearly the entire population' and 'killed or enslaved every Christian' differ in strength; I used the first, milder form.
490/491 riots: the two narrative traditions differ (who was attacked, whether one or two phases); I gave only the common point that the Greens attacked Jews, and said the accounts differ.
Founding legends: the eagle story is attributed to Malalas and Libanius. Iopolis, Kasiotis and Herakleia are named, with the article's 'no proof'.

Principality of Antioch: the article's text from 1100 to 1268 is a long chain of regents; I named only Bohemond, Tancred and Raymond of Poitiers and said 'at times as a vassal of the Byzantine emperors', as the article does for 1156.

Left out as not in the article's history: any present population figure for Antakya; the Habib-i Nejjar Mosque and the 2016 skeleton mosaic (present-day pilgrimage and a find, not history); the Alawite settlers and the Barker family; the Julian episode and the 387 sedition, for space.
'Hatay Province in southern Turkey': the article says 'Hatay Province in south Turkey'.
The facts 'known' line mentions 'repeated earthquakes' and 'Daphne' as the article does; the 'golden age' of the fourth and fifth centuries is the article's phrase for the mosaics.
